steps.body:
A Taylor series does not always work.

**1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + …** is perfect near 0 — and **useless** at x = 2, where it claims 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … equals −1.

There is a boundary. Inside it the polynomial hugs the curve; outside it, the terms grow and the whole thing runs away. That boundary is the **radius of convergence**.

widget.prompt: 1/(1 − x) with eight terms. Drag the evaluation point outward and find the SMALLEST x at which the terms xᵏ stop shrinking.
widget.successFeedback: x = 1. Below it the terms shrink and the polynomial hugs the curve; at exactly 1 every term is 1 — dead level, never fading — and beyond it they GROW. That is the radius of convergence, and you did not solve for it: you WATCHED the approximation give up. The dashed lines at ±1 are the boundary, and nothing you do with more terms will get you past them.
widget.lowFeedback: The terms are still shrinking here, so the series still converges — the polynomial is still hugging the curve. Push further out.
widget.highFeedback: The terms are growing here, so it has already given up — but you have overshot. Come back to the SMALLEST x where the shrinking stops.

predict.prompt: What does adding another correct Taylor term guarantee near the center?
predict.reveal: Each added term matches another derivative at the center, improving the local approximation without promising global equality.

cml.actionGoal: Add local derivative information term by term and compare a polynomial approximation with its target function.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the controlling quantity in this taylorApprox away from the successful state. Which invariant remains true, and which visible consequence changes?

explanation.prompt: Why is a Taylor polynomial strongest near its center?

options.label: Its coefficients are chosen to match successive derivatives there.
options.feedback: Exactly—this identifies the governing mechanism rather than only the final pattern.

options.label: Every high-degree polynomial is exact near zero.
options.feedback: That describes an appearance or shortcut, not the invariant that makes the relationship hold.

options.label: The curves merely look similar on the screen.
options.feedback: The live model contradicts that claim when its control is changed.

steps.body: More terms will not save you.
explanationVariants: Outside the radius, each new term is BIGGER than the last, so adding terms makes the polynomial worse, not better. No number of terms can rescue it.
This is the crucial difference from ordinary approximation error: inside the radius more terms always help; outside, they actively hurt.

widget.prompt: At x = 2, the series 1 + x + x² + … has terms 1, 2, 4, 8, … What happens if you add more terms?

options.label: It gets WORSE — each term is bigger than the last, so the sum runs away.
options.feedback: Right, and that is what makes the radius a hard boundary rather than a soft one. Outside it, more terms actively hurt.

options.label: It slowly improves.
options.feedback: The terms are DOUBLING. Every one you add pushes the sum further from the true value of 1/(1 − 2) = −1.

options.label: It converges to −1 eventually.
options.feedback: −1 is the value of the FUNCTION there, and the series has no way of reaching it. The two have simply parted company.

options.label: It stays the same.
options.feedback: Each new term adds a larger amount than the one before, so the partial sums climb without bound.

steps.body: Find the radius with the ratio test.
explanationVariants: The ratio of consecutive terms of Σxⁿ is |x|. The ratio test demands that be under 1, so the series converges exactly when |x| < 1: the radius is 1.
The ratio test does not merely test a series — pointed at a POWER series, it hands you the radius directly.

widget.prompt: For Σxⁿ, the ratio of consecutive terms is |x|. What is the radius of convergence?

commonErrors.feedback: A radius of 0 would mean it converges only at the centre. But at x = 0.5 the terms shrink beautifully, so the radius is larger than that.
At x = 2 the terms 1, 2, 4, 8 GROW, so the series has already failed there. The boundary is at 1.
At x = 0.5 the series converges perfectly well (to 2). The boundary is further out, at 1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The ratio test needs |x| < 1, so the radius is exactly 1.

steps.body:
And now the contrast that makes the point.

**eˣ** has an n! in every denominator. The ratio of consecutive terms is |x|/(n + 1) — which goes to **0 for every x**. The factorials always win, so the radius is **infinite**.

**1/(1 − x)** has no factorials. Its ratio is just |x|, which needs |x| < 1.

The factorial is the difference between a series that never gives up and one that does.

explanationVariants: The ratio |x|/(n + 1) shrinks to 0 no matter how big x is — the denominator eventually outruns any fixed numerator. So eˣ's series converges everywhere.
Even at x = 1000, the terms eventually collapse: once n passes 1000, each term is smaller than the last.

widget.prompt: For eˣ, the ratio of consecutive terms is |x|/(n + 1). Why is the radius infinite?

options.label: However big x is, the (n + 1) eventually outruns it — so the ratio goes to 0 for every x.
options.feedback: Right. Even at x = 1000, once n passes 1000 the terms start collapsing. The factorials always win in the end.

options.label: Because eˣ is always positive.
options.feedback: Sign has nothing to do with it. 1/(1 − x) is positive near 0 too, and it still has a finite radius.

options.label: Because e is irrational.
options.feedback: Irrationality is irrelevant. What matters is the factorial in the denominator, which crushes the terms.

options.label: It is not infinite — the radius is 1.
options.feedback: Try the widget at any x you like: the eˣ polynomial keeps hugging. The factorials mean it never gives up.

steps.body: Read the radius off the ratio.
hints: For Σ xⁿ/2ⁿ, write out the ratio of consecutive terms.
It is |x|/2, and the ratio test needs that under 1.
explanationVariants: It is a geometric series in disguise, with ratio x/2 — and geometric series converge exactly when the ratio is under 1 in magnitude.

widget.prompt: Find the radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/2ⁿ.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the radius for Σxⁿ. Dividing by 2ⁿ makes the terms shrink twice as fast, which pushes the boundary out to 2.
You may have inverted the ratio. |x|/2 < 1 gives |x| < 2, not |x| < 1/2.
Check the ratio: it is |x|/2, not |x|/4. The condition |x|/2 < 1 gives |x| < 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The ratio is |x|/2, so |x| < 2: the radius is 2.

takeaways: Inside the radius, more terms always help. OUTSIDE it, more terms make things worse — the boundary is hard, not soft.
The ratio test, pointed at a power series, hands you the radius directly.
Factorials in the denominator crush the terms and give an infinite radius. Without them, the radius is finite.
steps.teaser: That is BC series. Last course: parametric and polar curves, differentiated and integrated.

concept.body: Look at the terms at the x you care about. **Shrinking?** The series converges there and more terms help. **Growing?** It has given up, and no number of terms will bring it back. The boundary between the two is the radius.

explanationVariants: At x = 3 the terms of Σxⁿ are 1, 3, 9, 27 — growing. The series has given up.

widget.prompt: At x = 3, the terms of 1 + x + x² + … are 1, 3, 9, 27, … Does the series converge?

options.label: No — the terms are growing, so it diverges.
options.feedback: Right. Terms that grow can never be summed, and no number of them will help.

options.label: Yes, slowly.
options.feedback: Each term is three times the last. The partial sums race away to infinity.
